Introduction/Organisation transformation

Development guide

Organisation transformation

Adopting AI-assisted development changes how teams work, learn and review results. Plan changes across people, process, culture and technology, assign ownership for shared services, then use pilot evidence to decide what to adopt.

AI-assisted development means using AI to support development work. The resulting software does not need to contain AI.

On this page
Why tools alone are not enough Four areas that change together People Team composition Process Culture Technology Shared service ownership Run a pilot and decide from evidence Sources

Why tools alone are not enough

A team may draft code faster while completed changes still wait for clarification, review or release. Improving that workflow requires attention to the whole path from a user need to a working result. DORA’s 2025 report describes AI as amplifying existing organisational strengths and weaknesses.

McKinsey’s 2025 survey found that most organisations in its AI high-performer group were redesigning workflows. While these self-reported findings do not prove that workflow redesign leads to better results, they highlight it as a common practice among high-performing organisations.

Measure the effect in your own setting. METR’s early-2025 randomised study of 16 experienced open-source developers, completing 246 tasks in familiar repositories, found that AI use increased completion time by 19%. Participants nevertheless estimated that AI had saved them time.

That result is specific to those tools, tasks and developers. In February 2026, METR reported that selection effects and time-measurement problems made its follow-up data unreliable for estimating current productivity gains. Neither study supplies a forecast for your squad.

Start with one recurring delay or quality problem. Trial an AI-assisted workflow alongside the skills and controls it needs, then compare the results before expanding it.

Sources: [1]; [2]; [3]; [4].

Four areas that change together

Use these four areas to plan changes across people, process, culture and technology.

One upload-flow pilot: People produces a reviewed task brief and a named reviewer; Process produces acceptance checks and a decision record; Culture produces a short failure review with an owned correction; Technology provides test storage, limited permissions and a tested recovery procedure.

The diagram connects each area to the same way of working. People need skills to assess results; process defines checks and decisions; culture supports reporting problems; technology limits access and supports recovery. A pilot can start small while addressing all four.

Questions to answer before a pilot
AreaPlanning questionUseful output
PeopleWho can specify, perform and review the task?Named participants, skill gaps and coaching time
ProcessWhat evidence supports progress, and who decides?A task flow with checks and decision authority
CultureHow will people raise concerns and learn from failures?A feedback route and a review date
TechnologyWhat can the tool access, change and recover?Access limits, action records and a recovery method

An AI agent uses a model to choose or adapt actions and tool use towards a goal, within agreed permissions and limits. Agent-specific guidance below applies when tools act on systems, rather than only suggest text to a person.

People: broaden skills and retain specialist judgement

AI-assisted work still needs people who understand the user’s problem and can recognise an incorrect result. Build enough shared knowledge for colleagues to work across tasks, while preserving access to specialist review.

Develop breadth alongside depth

A T-shaped practitioner combines deep expertise in one field with enough breadth to collaborate across the lifecycle. Use this as a development goal, not an expectation that one person can replace a multidisciplinary team.

Observe the practice: breadth means a developer can trace one user requirement through implementation, testing and operational evidence, and recognise when to ask for help. Depth means a security specialist can explain a failed access-control test and verify the correction.

The horizontal bar represents skills shared across the team, such as specifying work, testing results and supervising AI tools. The vertical stem represents depth in a field such as security, design or data. Both are needed to judge when specialist help is necessary.

Make review responsibilities explicit

Agree who contributes to each change and what evidence they provide.

Example contributions to an AI-assisted change
RoleContribution and recorded output
Product ownerDefine the user need, scope and acceptance criteria; record whether the result meets them.
DesignerTest the experience with users; record usability and accessibility findings.
Technical leadReview architectural trade-offs and task boundaries; record decisions that affect other systems.
DeveloperGive the tool a bounded task; check the change and record test results and unresolved issues.
Platform / Cloud EngineerSet up and maintain continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines; provision and harden infrastructure; monitor operations and application health with developers. Retain pipeline results, reviewed infrastructure changes, hardening checks, dashboards and recovery evidence.
Quality assurance specialistAssess behaviour, reliability and test coverage; record exploratory findings, defects and gaps in acceptance evidence.
Security specialistAssess threats, data exposure and permission boundaries; record security findings and whether proposed controls address them.

Quality assurance (QA) and security collaborate, but answer different questions. QA assesses whether behaviour and reliability meet agreed criteria; security assesses threats and the effectiveness of protective controls. Record their acceptance responsibilities separately under the existing process. A QA acceptance does not grant security approval, and a security review does not establish functional acceptance. Route unresolved risks to the person authorised to accept them.

Learn through supported practice

Reserve time for coached work on a low-risk task. Pair a learner with someone able to review the result, and include a flawed output so the learner can practise detecting errors. Assess the specification, verification and explanation of limits, as well as the completed work.

Team leads can collect recurring skill gaps; whoever coordinates training can use that evidence to arrange coaching and share worked examples. Avoid treating tool usage or course completion alone as proof of competence.

Next step: choose one repeated task. Name who will specify it, who will review it and which skill each person needs to practise.

Team composition: towards human–agent teams

As agents take on more bounded tasks, a squad can become a human–agent team. People set intent, define boundaries, verify results and make decisions. Agents carry out delegated work such as research, prototyping, coding and test generation.

Agents hold no organisational accountability. Every agent task has a person who delegated it and a person who decides on the result.

Name the accountable task owner for each delegation and the person authorised to accept its result. The roles and agent capabilities are examples, not a staffing ratio. Retain diffs, test results and unresolved questions so the responsible person can review the work.

Build on existing expertise

AI-assisted work adds responsibilities to established professional expertise. Use the examples below to agree development needs for the work each person actually does. Assess competence through observed decisions and reviewed outputs.

Existing expertise, additional responsibilities and observable competence.
RoleExisting expertiseAdditional responsibilitiesObservable work
Product managerDiscovery, product strategy, prioritisation and outcome evaluationClarify intent for AI-assisted tasks; define evaluation criteria and exclusions.Identifies a flawed specification, resolves conflicting needs and rejects an outcome claim based on incomplete evidence.
UI/UX designerUser research, interaction design, accessibility and usability evaluationEvaluate generated experiences and failure states; guide prototypes with design tokens.Finds a misleading interaction or accessibility failure and tests the correction with relevant users.
Technical leadArchitecture, system trade-offs, engineering guidance and code reviewReview agent task boundaries, integration risks and the suitability of the harness.Detects an unsafe permission boundary, requests missing evidence and involves a security or platform specialist when needed.
DeveloperSoftware design, implementation, debugging, testing and operationsSpecify bounded tasks; inspect agent actions; verify changes against requirements.Finds a specification error repeated in generated code and tests, checks the correction and escalates beyond their expertise.
Platform / Cloud EngineerCI/CD automation, cloud infrastructure, networking, identity, hardening, monitoring and service recoveryReview AI-generated pipeline and infrastructure changes; bound deployment permissions; maintain automated controls and operational visibility.Rejects an over-permissive deployment change, demonstrates a blocked pipeline check, verifies infrastructure hardening and tests that an application failure triggers an actionable alert and recovery procedure.
QA specialistTest strategy, exploratory testing, reliability and defect analysisMaintain evaluation cases for AI-assisted work; assess generated tests and gaps in evidence.Identifies a missing failure case, reproduces a defect and records whether quality acceptance criteria are met.
Security specialistThreat modelling, access control, security testing and risk assessmentAssess agent tools, data flows, prompt injection and isolation controls.Demonstrates an unsafe permission boundary, verifies the control and routes residual risk to the authorised decision-maker.

Include Platform / Cloud Engineer capacity from planning through operation, either within the squad or through a named shared platform team. Agree the boundary between shared infrastructure and application responsibilities, with a support route and deputy. Developers add application health signals and diagnose code failures; platform engineers maintain the delivery and monitoring foundations. QA checks behaviour and reliability; security reviews threats and controls. Release and risk decisions follow the existing authorities.

Everyone needs to recognise incomplete evidence and know when to involve a specialist. Multi-agent orchestration is an optional specialism for people whose tasks require it; it is not a mastery target for every developer. Assign it with time for integration, review and recovery.

Terms used in these examples

  • PRD (product requirements document): the problem, users, scope and acceptance criteria for a product change.
  • TRD (technical requirements document): how the change will be built, including architecture, interfaces, data and constraints. A developer writes it as the blueprint for agent tasks, and the tech lead reviews it before agents start.
  • Design-token system: named values for colour, type and spacing, so that interfaces produced by agents stay consistent with the approved design.
  • Agent harness: the instructions, tools, permissions and checks that bound an agent’s work. Read about harness engineering.
  • Subagent orchestration: splitting work into bounded tasks for several agents, running dependent tasks in sequence and independent tasks in parallel where appropriate, and integrating their results.
  • Trajectory debugging: examining the sequence of steps, tool calls and decisions an agent took, to find where it went wrong.
  • Tier-1 and Tier-2 review: two layers of review. The developer reviews and verifies agent output first (Tier 1); the tech lead then reviews the developer’s submission (Tier 2).
  • Automated red-teaming and sandbox safety: probing a system automatically with adversarial inputs such as prompt injection, and running agent work in isolated environments with limited access.
  • LLM security: protecting systems that use a large language model (LLM) against risks such as prompt injection, data leakage and excessive permissions.

Make the transition in steps

A squad does not become a human–agent team in one move. Change team composition one task at a time, alongside the task permissions in the process section and the evidence from a pilot.

  1. Discuss the table with each squad member, and agree one additional responsibility to practise and the work that will demonstrate competence.
  2. Start with advice-only or isolated tasks, where a person reviews every result.
  3. Pair each learner with someone who can review their work; for example, a tech lead reviewing a developer’s first TRD.
  4. Widen an agent’s scope only when the evidence supports it and the person with authority agrees.

Example · fictional team

A developer who previously implemented features by hand writes a TRD for a search filter change, and the tech lead reviews it before any agent starts. The developer dispatches three bounded tasks to coding subagents on isolated branches: the filter logic, its tests and the documentation update.

The developer reviews each diff and test result (Tier 1), integrates them and opens a merge request, which the tech lead reviews (Tier 2). No agent can merge or deploy.

The Platform / Cloud Engineer configures the pipeline checks and a test environment. With the developer, they add a health check for the search journey, test its alert and rehearse rollback before the authorised release decision.

Parallel agents increase the volume of work to review. Delegate only as many tasks as the team can verify properly; unreviewed output is not progress.

Choose team size and specialist coverage from workload, risk and review capacity. Smaller teams and greater agent autonomy are not measures of maturity.

Next step: with each squad member, pick the table row closest to their role. Agree one additional responsibility to practise on the next low-risk task, what evidence will demonstrate it and who will review the result.

Process: connect checks to decisions

Map the existing workflow before changing it. Separate time spent doing work from time waiting for information, review or approval. A slow checkpoint may need clearer inputs or more review capacity, rather than automation.

Keep the purpose of each control visible

  1. Ask the person responsible for the control what outcome it protects.
  2. Record the evidence needed and which checks can assess it reliably.
  3. Confirm who can authorise progress and when a person needs to intervene.

A passing check provides evidence for the authorised decision. Record acceptance or rework with its reason; unresolved failures do not become a pass. Review lessons before changing rules or thresholds.

Set authority for the specific task

Choose agent permissions according to impact, reversibility and the evidence available. IMDA’s Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI discusses bounding risk and keeping agents traceable and controllable. Its May 2026 update adds deployment case studies.

Example task permissions; these are options, not a progression to full autonomy
Task boundaryAgent actionHuman decision
Advice onlyDraft a recommendation without changing a system.A person checks the advice and decides whether to act.
Isolated changeEdit a branch and run tests using limited permissions.A reviewer assesses the change before it enters a shared system.
Pre-authorised routine actionPerform an explicitly permitted action after defined checks pass.An authorised person sets the scope and stop conditions; the team monitors results.
High-impact or uncertain actionPrepare evidence within its permitted scope.An authorised person decides before execution; the agent stops if authority is missing.

Record who delegated the task, its scope, the evidence and the outcome. Protect these records under the applicable data-handling rules. Escalate failed checks, unexpected access requests and changes outside scope.

Next step: document one checkpoint’s purpose, required evidence and decision authority. Review the proposed change with the person responsible for that control.

Sources: [5]; [6].

Culture: make learning and accountability visible

People need to be able to question AI output, report failures and ask for help without pressure to demonstrate speed gains. DORA links high trust and effective information flow with stronger software delivery and organisational performance.

Explain the change and listen to concerns

Before a pilot, the team lead can explain its purpose, how responsibilities may change and how results will be assessed. Invite concerns about workload, skills and review effort. Record unanswered questions and assign someone to follow them up.

DORA’s AI Capabilities Model identifies a clearly communicated position on AI use as a supporting capability. Make permitted tools, data boundaries and the route for questions easy to find. Agree these with the relevant organisational owners.

Agree what acceptable work looks like

Set acceptance criteria before the task starts. Use tests for behaviour that can be checked automatically and human review for contextual judgement. An AI-generated assessment can help a reviewer, but it can also be wrong.

For each change, record whether the criteria were met, which risks remain and who can decide on them. Where recovery matters, check the recovery method. Passing tests alone does not demonstrate that a change is useful, secure or ready to release.

Turn failures into improvements

At a retrospective, examine the task instructions, available context, tool permissions and review evidence. Agree a specific improvement, an owner and a completion date. Recognise useful escalation and defects caught during review, as well as successful delivery.

Next step: discuss one failed AI-assisted task with the people involved. Choose one improvement to a test, instruction or control, and record who will make it.

Sources: [7]; [8].

Technology: provide bounded access and recovery

Build on existing repositories, delivery pipelines and access controls. Start with the capabilities needed for the pilot; a new platform is not a prerequisite. When an agent can act, make its permissions and actions attributable to the task and the person who authorised it.

OWASP recommends limiting tool functionality, permissions and autonomy, with authorisation enforced by the connected systems rather than the model. Prompts alone are not an access-control boundary.

Check the platform’s support for the task

Suggested capabilities and how to check them
CapabilityPractical check
Relevant contextGive the tool current requirements and approved reference material; record their versions and restrict access to what the task needs.
Identity and permissionsUse scoped credentials or delegated access that preserves the user’s authority limits. Check that unauthorised actions are denied.
Isolated executionSeparate experimental work from shared systems. Limit tool access, execution time and spending.
VerificationRun tests against acceptance criteria. Compare a sample of AI assessments with qualified reviewers and investigate disagreement.
Action recordsRecord changes, tool calls, versions and outcomes with appropriate access and retention controls; avoid unnecessary sensitive content.
RecoveryTest stopping a run, revoking access and restoring affected state. Identify actions that cannot be undone.

DORA’s capabilities research associates useful internal platforms and access to relevant internal data with stronger AI benefits. This supports improving context and platform quality; it does not justify unrestricted data access.

Build, harden and operate the delivery path

The Platform / Cloud Engineer connects delivery automation with reliable service operation. Agree these responsibilities with the application team and existing platform and security owners:

  • CI/CD pipelines: configure repeatable builds, tests, security checks and deployment stages, with scoped deployment credentials and retained results. Demonstrate that a failed check blocks promotion and rehearse rollback. Use the EDS pipeline stages when applying the EDS workflow.
  • Infrastructure setup and hardening: provision environments through reviewed, version-controlled infrastructure as code, which describes resources and configuration in files. Apply agreed identity, network, secrets and patching controls. Record hardening checks, track configuration drift and test restoration from backups where needed.
  • Operations and application health: work with developers to collect metrics, logs and traces, and check important user journeys. Agree service health targets; monitor availability, latency, errors and resource capacity. Test alert routing to a named responder and maintain runbooks with diagnosis, escalation and recovery steps.

AI tools can draft pipeline definitions, infrastructure changes and runbooks, or summarise operational evidence. Review generated changes and test them in an isolated environment before authorised promotion. Grant agents permissions for their delegated task; agree separately who can deploy, change production infrastructure or respond to incidents.

Supporting guidance: [10]; [11]; [12].

Keep verification independent of generation

Combine automated tests with specialist review according to the task’s risk. An agent’s explanation that its own work is correct is not independent evidence. Review the test cases too: tests generated from a misunderstood requirement may repeat the same error.

A merge request can collect code-change evidence, but other actions need controls at their own point of execution. Data access, deployment and external communications may happen outside a code review. Enforce permissions where those actions occur.

Assign ownership for shared services

Squad pilots depend on shared services that need ongoing maintenance. Map the responsibilities below to existing roles, and name an owner and a deputy or support route before wider adoption.

Shared service ownership before wider adoption
ResponsibilityOwner to identifyWork to maintain
Shared harnessPlatform or engineering maintainerVersion instructions, tools and integrations; test changes, publish releases and keep a rollback route.
CI/CD pipelinesPlatform / Cloud Engineer, with application engineering and QAMaintain build and deployment stages, runners, credentials, enforced checks, release evidence and rollback procedures.
Infrastructure and hardeningPlatform / Cloud Engineer, with platform and security ownersMaintain infrastructure code, environment separation, access and network controls, patching, hardening evidence, drift checks and recovery tests.
Operations and application healthPlatform / Cloud Engineer and application service owner, with developersMaintain health signals, dashboards, alerts and runbooks; agree responders, support coverage and escalation. Review incidents and feed findings into delivery work.
Approved modelsModel service owner, working with security, privacy and procurementMaintain permitted models and uses, data terms, access limits and costs; evaluate upgrades and provide migration notice.
Policy contentThe owner of each applicable policy or controlKeep authoritative guidance current, version changes and resolve conflicts. Harness maintainers implement agreed controls.
Evaluation datasetsEvaluation owner, with domain, QA and security reviewersMaintain representative tasks, expected outcomes, adversarial cases, access rights and version history; investigate gaps and rerun checks after changes.
SupportService support ownerPublish a help route, triage failures, maintain known issues and provide coaching or specialist escalation.
Incident responseExisting service and security incident ownersAgree who can stop runs and revoke access, preserve evidence, recover service, communicate impact and authorise resumption.
Ongoing fundingAccountable budget ownerFund model use, maintenance, evaluation, support and incident capacity; review total cost and decide whether continued funding is justified.

Keep this ownership record with the shared service documentation, including contacts, capacity, funding and review dates. Squad leads report gaps to these owners; service owners publish changes and known limits to affected squads. A pilot lead does not automatically inherit responsibility for the shared platform.

Next step: list one agent’s tools, data access and permissions. With the system owner, remove unnecessary access and test recovery. Before wider adoption, complete the shared ownership record and confirm maintenance capacity and funding.

Sources: [9]; [8].

Run a pilot and decide from evidence

Choose one recurring task with a clear outcome and manageable consequences if it fails. Name a pilot lead to collect evidence and confirm who can decide whether the workflow continues.

  1. Establish a baseline. Record completion time, review effort, rework and quality for comparable recent tasks. Define where timing starts and ends.
  2. Define the trial. Record the tool and version, task boundaries, permitted data, reviewers, acceptance criteria and stop conditions. Agree scorecard thresholds, an observation period for escaped defects and the person authorised to decide on adoption before results are known. For trials affecting a running service, name platform and application responders and test alerting and recovery.
  3. Run a small batch. Include unsuccessful attempts and recovery effort in the record. Ask participants what helped and what added work.
  4. Review the evidence. Compare results with the baseline, noting differences in task difficulty and team experience. A small before-and-after comparison can guide a decision but does not establish causation.
  5. Publish the decision. Share the scorecard and the decision to expand, restrict, continue testing or retire the capability with affected teams, subject to data-handling rules. Record the decision-maker, evidence, limits and next review date; reassess after material model, harness or workflow changes.

Publish baseline and trial results side by side for each comparable task type, with sample sizes, tool versions, thresholds and limitations. Separate task types and risk levels so a favourable average cannot hide failures in a particular use. Include abandoned attempts and record missing evidence as unknown.

A suggested pilot scorecard; set local thresholds before the trial
MeasureRecord and interpret
Comparable task typesTask scope, complexity, risk, repository familiarity and participant experience; baseline and trial counts, including failures. Explain differences that limit comparison.
User outcomeWhether the result met acceptance criteria and helped the intended user. Faster output without a useful result is not a success.
Delivery timeElapsed time to an accepted result, waiting time and active human effort, using the same start and end points for both workflows.
Review effortHuman time checking specifications, generated work and evaluation evidence, including specialist reviews and repeat review rounds.
ReworkCorrection time, rejected outputs, repeated runs and recovery effort, including work abandoned without an accepted result.
Escaped defects and riskDefects found after acceptance, their severity and user impact over the agreed observation period; failed controls, incidents and recovery outcomes. Review serious failures individually.
Operational readiness and healthPipeline failures, infrastructure hardening findings, application availability, latency and errors; alert response and recovery results against agreed targets. Name the operational owner and record gaps before expanding.
Total costModel and tool charges, infrastructure, pipeline and monitoring services, setup, training, human work, shared harness maintenance, evaluation, support and incidents. Count each cost once and include failed attempts; report total cost and cost per accepted result.
Developer experienceParticipant feedback on cognitive load, interruptions, trust, learning and ability to challenge output. Pair feedback with observed work and escalation reasons; fewer escalations can reflect missed problems.

Agree what the evidence permits

Before the pilot, agree numerical thresholds, required controls and who decides on functional acceptance, security approval and wider adoption. Use the rules below to decide the next step.

  • Expand: comparable tasks meet the agreed outcome, quality, cost and experience thresholds, including review and rework; the defect observation period is complete and required controls pass. Confirm shared service owners, funding and review capacity. Expand only to the task types and permissions supported by that evidence.
  • Restrict: benefits hold only for some task types, or review burden, defects or control failures exceed a threshold. Narrow scope or permissions, restore human checks and require a new evaluation before reconsidering the excluded uses. Stop affected actions immediately when a stop condition is met.
  • Retire: repeated evaluated revisions fail the agreed thresholds, a required control cannot be maintained, or ongoing cost and support cannot be justified. The authorised owner withdraws the capability, removes its access and returns work to a supported workflow.
  • Continue testing: the sample is too small, tasks are not comparable or follow-up evidence is incomplete. Keep the existing boundary, name the missing evidence and set a bounded extension with a review date.

Example · fictional pilot

A squad trials an agent that drafts regression tests on an isolated branch. The developer checks the tests against acceptance criteria; a reviewer decides whether to merge them. The agent has no merge or deployment permission.

The pilot lead publishes baseline and trial results for comparable regression-test tasks: completion time, review effort, rework, escaped defects, total cost and developer feedback. If review effort removes the expected saving, the squad restricts the trial and evaluates a revision. Expansion waits for the agreed thresholds and defect observation period, with a named harness owner and funded support.

Allow for setup and learning costs, and set a review date so a pilot does not continue indefinitely. Higher autonomy is an option, not a success measure; a useful advisory workflow may remain advisory.

Next step: write a short pilot brief covering the task, participants, baseline, boundaries, success criteria and review date. Use the DORA capability guidance to identify supporting improvements, and read the Concepts guide for ways to specify and supervise AI-assisted work.

Source: [8].
